Is gen-AI already reshaping the French labor market? 

Recruitment may respond to technological change before total employment, as firms reduce hiring or stop replacing departing staff. This adjustment is particularly relevant in France, where permanent contract terminations are more strictly regulated.

Combining an occupation-level AI exposure index tailored to the French labour market with comprehensive data on labour market flows, we find that:

1) Between late 2022 and March 2026, permanent hires of 21–29-year-olds fell by around 28% in the most AI-exposed occupations, versus 8% in the least exposed. This hiring gap narrows with age and nearly disappears among workers aged 50 and over.

2) Permanent contract terminations among 21–29-year-olds also fell more sharply in the most AI-exposed occupations, indicating lower labour turnover.

3) Firms reporting intensive AI use saw a sharper decline in young workers’ permanent hires than other firms, particularly in the most AI-exposed occupations. This was not accompanied by a divergence in total employment.

As for other countries, these trends coincide with other shocks (business cycle, remote work) and do not establish a causal effect of AI. But they warrant close monitoring, as automating entry-level tasks could reduce opportunities to learn on the job and develop skills over time.

Full report in French: https://shorturl.at/ghdBy

Behind the showroom, everything ran on Excel sheets and WhatsApp groups, and nothing connected any of it.

That is when the tracker became Trackaroo, one platform for a dealership’s sales, leads and approvals. They kept it fast and simple, and dealers started recommending it to each other. 

Today it runs dealership operations for brands like Tata, KTM, Ather and Royal Enfield. Its AI layer, SanjAI, even lets owners ask plain questions about their business and get instant answers.

That traction is what took Trackaroo to BITS Pilani. Pratyush applied to its Gen AI Accelerator and cleared the first round. In round two, he had 20 minutes to pitch and the rest for questions on traction, competitors and pricing.

People often fear making a bad hire more than they desire making a good one.

For a buyer, a poor hire can create costs beyond the invoice: lost time, a missed deadline or an awkward conversation with their team. A proposal that only celebrates the upside may leave those concerns unanswered. Show how you will recognize problems, keep progress visible and make review manageable.

A launch team may worry more about missing its date than receiving an additional feature. A credible schedule, dependency list and review plan address that concern directly. Adding another bonus to the proposal may leave the real obstacle untouched.

1. Ask what went wrong in previous projects.
2. Connect your evidence to the risks the buyer names.
3. Explain the review points before work starts.
4. Set realistic responsibilities for both sides rather than promising that nothing can go wrong.

Confidence grows when the client can understand the route through the project, including the difficult parts. Address the concern they are carrying into the decision.

What risk do your clients ask about most often?

Every real-time application depends on a constant flow of events.

Apache Kafka helps move those events reliably between systems, 
making it a core technology for modern data platforms, streaming analytics, & AI applications.

◈ Data Sources
↳ Events are generated from applications, databases, APIs, IoT devices, and business systems
↳ Every click, transaction, update, or sensor reading becomes an event

◈ Producers
↳ Producer applications publish events to Kafka topics
↳ Services built with Java, Python, Node.js, Spark, and other technologies can send data into Kafka

◈ Kafka Cluster
↳ Topics organize events such as Orders, Payments, Customers, Inventory, and Clickstream data
↳ Partitions distribute data across brokers for scalability
↳ Replication keeps data available even if a broker fails

◈ Consumer Groups
↳ Multiple applications can read the same events independently
↳ Analytics platforms, fraud detection systems, and recommendation engines can all consume the same stream

◈ Stream Processing
↳ Kafka Streams, Apache Flink, and Spark Structured Streaming process events in real time
↳ Data can be filtered, enriched, aggregated, and transformed as it flows through the platform

◈ Analytics & AI
↳ Event streams power dashboards, reporting, machine learning models, vector databases, AI agents, and RAG applications
↳ The same data can support both operational systems and AI workloads

◈ Governance & Security
↳ Schema Registry, monitoring, access control, lineage, and data contracts help keep data reliable and consistent

One of Kafka's biggest advantages is that producers & consumers remain independent of each other.

New applications can start consuming existing event streams without changing the systems that produce them,
making it easier to scale and evolve over time.

Effective October 5, 2026, Spain’s Royal Decree 723/2026 dramatically expands the information companies must provide to employees in writing. Replacing regulations in place since 1998, this decree demands exhaustive transparency before the employment relationship begins, fundamentally changing standard onboarding procedures. 

-Algorithmic Transparency (AI): Companies must explicitly disclose if automated systems, algorithms, or AI influence shift scheduling, task assignments, variable pay, career progression, or contract terminations. 
-Granular Compensation Data: It is no longer sufficient to state a lump-sum salary. Base pay and supplements must be separated, and the exact calculation criteria for variable pay, bonuses, and commissions must be detailed. 
-Deepened Workplace Policies: Employers must provide information identifying the company's equality plan, work-life balance policies, sexual harassment protocols, and measures for LGBTQ+ inclusion. 
-Working Hours & Irregular Shifts: The contract or supplementary documentation must break down daily/weekly/annual hours, overtime rules, and the exact procedures for modifying or canceling shifts. 
-Retroactive Requests: While companies do not need to automatically reissue contracts for existing staff, current employees can request this expanded information at any time, triggering a strict 30-business-day deadline for the company to comply.

HR and Legal departments must urgently audit their standard contract templates and supplementary onboarding packets. Pinpoint exactly what automated HR tools are being used and document their operational criteria. Avoid compliance breaches by updating internal protocols before the next wave of hiring.

I participated in the Compass AI Tech Summit Conference last week. I’m happily sharing my thoughts on topics I listened to and that I found interesting to comment on.

The Trilemma: Buying Software vs. Hiring People vs. Deploying AI Agents 

Speaker: Eduards Ruzga - CEO and Co-founder at Desktop Commander 

Session: Software vs People vs AI Agents — Pricing, Security, UX 

Enterprises are caught in an operational pricing and security clash. Eduards Ruzga broke down the friction of enterprise AI agent adoption by comparing them against the two operational models enterprises already know how to manage: traditional SaaS subscriptions and human employees. 

AI agents sit uncomfortably in between: 

- Pricing Models: Traditional seat licenses don't work; token billing creates unpredictable cost spikes; outcome-based pricing is exceptionally difficult to define and audit. 

- Security Baselines: Traditional software runs within strict role-based access control (RBAC). Employees are bound by employment contracts, ethics, and background checks. An AI agent is a probabilistic actor with tool-calling execution rights inside your network. 

- UX and Onboarding: Managing agent expectations and onboarding them onto complex workflows requires a hybrid of HR-style training and API integration. 

Dilemmas on the rise: 
- Treating an agent like a standard SaaS tool ignores its non-deterministic execution risks. 
- Treating an agent like an employee ignores its lack of common sense, context, and legal liability. 
- Procurement and enterprise risk teams need an entirely new rubric for evaluating agentic platforms. 

Strategic Inquiries: 
- How is your finance organization modeling the financial variance of outcome-based and token-based agent workflows? 
- Who assumes liability in your vendor contracts when an autonomous third-party agent makes an erroneous operational decision?

The dangerous part of an enterprise AI agent often begins after the prompt looks ordinary.

An onboarding agent opens a PDF. A shopping assistant receives a normal request. Then the software calls an API, reaches into a system, follows an instruction nobody intended, or probes infrastructure at machine speed. The risk has already crossed into production.

That handoff is where Rein Security is placing its bet.

Matan Bar-Efrat, co-founder and CEO, and Netanel Rubin, co-founder and CTO, built Rein around runtime context: observe what an agent executes, which resources it touches, and whether the action should be allowed. Rein describes its platform as a patented sidecar that applies real-time guardrails while keeping data inside the customer's environment.

Rein has raised a $25M Series A co-led by Glilot Capital and Sienna Venture Capital, with Corner Ventures, Atlacle and RNP Capital Advisors participating. The company says the round brings total funding to $35M and will finance product work, agent-security research and global hiring.

The capital arrives behind early operating evidence, with a qualifier. Rein reports 8x revenue growth and 5x customer growth since its January 2026 launch, plus thousands of protected agents executing millions of actions. Flex, Swimlane, Lemonade and Dun & Bradstreet are named users. The absolute revenue, customer counts and contract values are not public.

The funding math deserves precision. Rein disclosed an $8M seed in January and a $25M Series A now. Those rounds total $33M, while the company reports $35M raised to date. The reviewed announcements do not identify the remaining $2M.

Investors are backing a category decision as much as a company. Gartner expects the market for securing AI to reach about $4.8B in 2027, up 68.7% from 2026. That opportunity will attract gateways, governance platforms, application-security vendors and every incumbent capable of adding an AI tab to a dashboard.

Rein's argument is more specific: prompt inspection is too early and post-incident review is too late. Security has to travel with the agent into the moment where language becomes access, code and business action.

The $25M gives Rein more room to prove that runtime control can become a durable enterprise budget line. The buyer's standard will be unforgiving: see enough to stop harmful action, preserve the context needed to explain it, and stay light enough that production teams will keep the control turned on.

About the Role
We're hiring a senior full-stack engineer to support and evolve our existing Microsoft-stack applications, own our Azure infrastructure and API management layer, and work as a first mover in adopting AI development tools (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot) as a core part of daily engineering practice. This is not a greenfield role — you'll be extending, hardening, and modernizing production .NET applications that the business already depends on, while pushing the team's tooling and delivery practices forward.

This role sits across the full stack — front end, C#/.NET backend, SQL Server, and Azure infrastructure — with genuine ownership of features end to end, not siloed hand-offs between specialists.

What You'll Do
Full-stack delivery: Design, build, and maintain features end to end across a modern frontend (React/TypeScript or equivalent), C#/.NET Web APIs, and SQL Server — owning the feature from design through production support.
Azure infrastructure & API management: Own and evolve our Azure footprint — App Service/Functions, Azure API Management (policies, versioning, rate limiting, gateway design), CI/CD via Azure DevOps, and infrastructure-as-code (Bicep/Terraform).

Support existing .NET applications: Maintain, refactor, and modernize our current production .NET applications — this includes bug triage, performance tuning, incremental modernization of legacy code, and production incident response, not just new-feature work.

AI-augmented development: Fully adopt AI coding tools (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or equivalent) as a daily part of your workflow — not as a novelty, but as a genuine productivity and quality lever, with sound judgment about when to trust, verify, or reject AI-generated output, especially in production-critical code paths.

Architecture & code quality: Apply sound design patterns and SOLID principles in real code, not just in theory; contribute to technical design decisions including API contracts, service boundaries, and messaging/command-query patterns (CQRS/MediatR) where appropriate.

Collaboration: Work closely with product owners, other engineers, and stakeholders; communicate technical tradeoffs clearly; mentor other engineers where relevant.

What should a founder expect from a CFO at an AI startup?

a16z’s “You Need a New CFO,” by Seema Amble, Ivan Makarov and David Borecky, makes a timely case: finance leaders increasingly design the systems through which the business operates.

My view: that responsibility brings accounting, commercial judgement and product understanding closer together.

The traditional responsibilities remain: reliable accounts, cash discipline, controls and capital allocation. The new mandate is to make them useful at the speed the business moves.

For an AI company, I would start with three questions.
1. Does more usage create more value—or just more cost?
A customer can expand usage while contributing less to the business. I want revenue connected to inference, cloud, implementation and support costs, with the assumptions visible.
That gives founders a basis for deciding which contracts to reprice, which workflows to improve and where growth deserves more investment.
2. Which decisions can an agent make, and who remains accountable?
Before automating a finance workflow, define the evidence required, approval thresholds, exception handling and the person responsible for the outcome.
An agent completing a task is only part of the test. The team must be able to explain and review what happened.
3. What would make us change the plan?
A forecast should help management act when usage, customer commitments or delivery costs change. I would connect those signals to hiring, pricing and spending decisions, with clear triggers for revisiting assumptions.

This is the direction of my work across Actnow, FINANCE KERNEL™ and my theses on AI Cost Governance and Scaling AI Infrastructure from Seed to IPO.

The common thread is building financial foundations around how an AI business actually earns revenue, consumes resources and makes decisions.
My work on finance-agent governance adds another dimension: translating finance judgement into workflows with explicit limits, evidence and human accountability.
After 15+ years across controllership, CFO and finance leadership, I want to bring that experience inside one ambitious AI company and take responsibility for building its next stage.

AI-native founders: which financial decision is hardest today—pricing, compute commitments, funding capacity ahead of demand, or understanding whether growth improves margins?

Investors across VC and PE: what financial capability do you most want your AI portfolio companies to build before their next stage of growth?
